text: The Mimi codec operates at a frame rate of 12.5 Hz and a bitrate of 1.1 kbps【M107】. The papers do not provide any other frame‑rate or bitrate values for Mimi.

Mimi uses eight residual vector quantizers, and each quantizer has a codebook of 2 048 centroids【M70】. The architecture description also notes that the latent space is discretized with Q quantizers, each with a codebook of NA centroids【M67】.
The Helium text‑only language model has about 7 billion parameters and was pretrained on roughly 2.1 trillion tokens [M106].
Moshi’s theoretical latency is 160 ms, and in practice it reaches about 200 ms [M38, M119].
The unsupervised audio dataset used for Moshi’s pre‑training contains 7 million hours of audio [M91].
Moshi was fine‑tuned on the Fisher dataset to gain its fully duplex capabilities [M61].
Moshi is pretrained with an acoustic delay of 2 steps, and then finetuned with an acoustic delay of 1 step [M119].

The Inner Monologue method first predicts time‑aligned text tokens as a prefix before generating the audio tokens [M38, M45]. The papers do not specify any other type of prediction made prior to the audio tokens.

H‑Net’s routing module computes a similarity score between each pair of adjacent encoder outputs by projecting them ( qₜ = W_q x̂ₜ, kₜ₋₁ = W_k x̂ₜ₋₁ ) and taking their cosine similarity; when the similarity is low, the resulting boundary probability pₜ = 1 − (qₜᵀkₜ₋₁)/(‖qₜ‖‖kₜ₋₁‖) becomes high, indicating a semantic shift and a likely chunk boundary [H221]. A hard boundary indicator bₜ is then set to 1 if pₜ ≥ 0.5, otherwise 0, with p₁ forced to 1 to start the sequence [H221]. The papers do not specify any additional heuristics beyond this similarity‑based scoring.
H‑Net builds its encoder and decoder networks from state‑space‑model (SSM) layers, often instantiated as Mamba layers, rather than pure Transformer blocks [H219][H216].

H‑Net’s language models were trained on the 100 billion‑token subset sampled from the FineWeb‑Edu dataset [H242] and each tokenizer‑free model processed 8 192 utf‑8‑encoded bytes per sequence [H242]. The papers do not state any other datasets or sequence lengths for these experiments.
On English, the space‑like delimiter heuristic averages about 6.0 bytes per chunk [H238].

H‑Net reports almost a four‑fold increase in data efficiency for DNA language modeling compared to baseline models [H201]. In another result it notes a 3.6× improvement in data efficiency over isotropic models for DNA tasks [H212]. The papers do not give a single unified figure beyond these reported multiples.
The base Transformer uses a model dimension \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) [T30].

The routing module measures the similarity between adjacent encoder output vectors and treats points where the cosine similarity drops (indicating a contextual or semantic shift) as likely chunk boundaries, converting these similarity scores into boundary probabilities [H525]. The module is a component of the chunking layer, which together with a downsampler forms the full chunking operation [H524]. The papers do not specify any additional heuristics beyond this similarity‑based decision.
H‑Net employs Mamba (Mamba‑2) layers for both its encoder and decoder networks, using them throughout all encoder and decoder components in the final configuration [H656].

H‑Net’s language models were trained on the 100 billion‑token subset sampled from the FineWeb‑Edu dataset, and each tokenizer‑free model processes 8 192 utf‑8‑encoded bytes per sequence [H584]. The papers do not provide any additional information about other datasets or data quantities.
The space-like delimiter heuristic averages about 6.0 bytes per chunk on English text [H572].

H‑Net reports that its 1‑stage model with an M3T1 encoder achieves about 3.6× higher data efficiency than an isotropic architecture on DNA language modeling [H761]. The abstract also notes a “nearly 4× improvement in data efficiency” for DNA compared with baselines [H477]. The papers do not give a more precise single figure beyond these reported multiples.

H‑Net’s routing module computes a similarity score between each pair of adjacent encoder output vectors by projecting them ( qₜ = W_q x̂ₜ, kₜ₋₁ = W_k x̂ₜ₋₁ ) and taking their cosine similarity; when the cosine similarity is low, the resulting boundary probability pₜ = 1 − (qₜ·kₜ₋₁)/(‖qₜ‖‖kₜ₋₁‖) becomes high, and a boundary is placed if pₜ ≥ 0.5 [H221]. The module therefore places chunk boundaries at points where adjacent representations diverge semantically, using this similarity‑based probability as the decision criterion [H207]. The papers do not specify any additional heuristics beyond this similarity‑based rule.

Training proceeded with a fixed compute budget of 256 examples per gradient step, each example containing 8 192 utf‑8‑encoded bytes, i.e., 8 192 bytes per sequence [H259]. H‑Net’s routing module decides chunk boundaries by computing a cosine‑similarity score between adjacent encoder outputs. For each position \(t\), it projects the current output \(\hat{x}_t\) into two vectors \(q_t=W_q\hat{x}_t\) and \(k_{t-1}=W_k\hat{x}_{t-1}\), then forms the boundary probability \(p_t=1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{\|q_t\|\|k_{t-1}\|}\). A boundary indicator \(b_t\) is set to 1 when \(p_t\ge 0.5\) (with \(p_1=1.0\) to start a boundary). This formulation turns low cosine similarity—indicating a semantic shift—into a high boundary probability, thereby placing chunk boundaries where adjacent representations diverge in latent space. [H221]
